Mapping the neuronal building blocks of human language with language models

A language network in the individualized functional connectomes of 1199 human brains doing arbitrary tasks

Phonological loop?

Human language rides on a set of cortical-subcortical circuits that are highly specialized for mapping signals to structure and meaning while remaining deeply integrated with more general control, memory, and sensorimotor systems. The best top-down description is a pair of large-scale pathways: a left-dominant dorsal stream that maps sound to articulation and an often bilateral ventral stream that maps sound to meaning (Hickok & Poeppel, 2007; Saur et al., 2008; Friederici, 2011/2012). The dorsal stream originates in posterior superior temporal cortex and area Spt at the temporo-parietal junction and projects via supramarginal/angular parietal cortex into premotor and inferior frontal articulatory regions; the ventral stream runs from mid/posterior superior temporal sulcus/gyrus into middle/anterior temporal lobe and onward to ventrolateral prefrontal cortex. White-matter anatomy supporting these streams includes long and indirect segments of the arcuate fasciculus and SLF dorsally, and the extreme capsule, inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus (IFOF), and uncinate fasciculus ventrally (Catani et al., 2005; Saur et al., 2008; Makris et al., 2009; Dick et al., 2012). In right-handed populations, dorsal long-segment asymmetry is common ( 82.5% leftward), consistent with left-lateralized phonological-articulatory control and bilateral but left-biased semantics (Catani et al., 2007; Binder et al., 2009; Friederici, 2011).

At the representational level, posterior-mid superior temporal regions host phonological codes and sublexical sequence structure, anterior temporal lobe functions as a transmodal "semantic hub" that integrates distributed conceptual features, and inferior frontal cortex supports unification operations over phonology, syntax, and semantics (Hagoort’s MUC model) (Lambon Ralph et al., 2017; Binder et al., 2009; Hagoort, 2013/2016). The ATL hub view explains broad semantic deficits in semantic dementia and converges with a "semantic control" network comprising left IFG and posterior middle temporal cortex that modulates retrieval when meaning must be shaped by task goals or context. Angular gyrus and anterior temporal pole contribute to multimodal integration at sentence/discourse scales, consistent with their long intrinsic timescales and coupling to default-mode subsystems during narratives (Lambon Ralph et al., 2017; Noonan et al., 2013; Humphreys & Lambon Ralph, 2015). A recent anatomical account diagrams the language network (Figure) 3. The same study reconstructs association pathways (Figure).

During speaking, cortical processing unfolds in a repeatable temporal cascade. Meta-analyses and chronometric studies estimate that lemma selection begins by  200 ms after cue onset, phonological code retrieval by  275 ms, syllabification by  350 ms, and phonetic/motor encoding  450-600 ms, mapping onto mid/posterior temporal, inferior parietal, and inferior frontal/premotor territories, with left anterior insula and ventral premotor cortex contributing to articulatory planning (Indefrey & Levelt, 2004/2011; Dronkers, 1996). The dorsal stream’s sensorimotor interface, area Spt, supports phonological working memory and auditory-motor transformations; its disruption yields conduction-aphasia-like phonological output errors and impaired nonword repetition, highlighting the role of dorsal buffers in on-the-fly sequence assembly (Hickok & Poeppel, 2007). These temporal-anatomical correspondences ground a mechanistic account: lexical access and morphosyntactic selection in temporal cortex feed dorsal phonological encoders and frontal unification/motor programs, with online self-monitoring via auditory predictions of one’s own speech.

Comprehension engages bilateral auditory cortex at phoneme-syllable timescales but rapidly recruits left mid/posterior STG/STS for phonological-to-lexical mapping and ventral temporal-frontal circuits for semantics and combinatorics (Hickok & Poeppel, 2007; Saur et al., 2008; Friederici, 2011). Two high-precision signatures constrain models of inference-time dynamics. First, cortical oscillations are organized by speech rhythms: delta-theta bands align with prosodic/ syllabic structure, while gamma relates to phonemic encoding, and cross-frequency coupling supports hierarchical parsing and prediction (Giraud & Poeppel, 2012; Ding et al., 2016). Second, event-related potentials index stages of meaning and structure building: N400 amplitudes track contextual predictability and semantic access (peaking  400 ms) and the P600 often reflects reanalysis or conflict at the form-meaning interface; both can co-occur when surprisal propagates across levels (Kutas & Federmeier, 2011; Kuperberg, 2007). Together these data support predictive, multi-level inference in which ventral circuits instantiate priors over lexical semantics and combinatorics while dorsal circuits maintain phonological items and serial constraints.

The production-perception loop is stabilized by forward models. During speaking, auditory cortex exhibits "speaking-induced suppression" and selective error responses when feedback is perturbed, consistent with corollary discharge from motor to sensory cortex that predicts self-generated sounds and gates error signals (Houde & Nagarajan, 2011). Intracranial and neuromodulatory studies refine the picture: suppression peaks in early auditory fields at utterance onset, prediction errors emerge when formants are shifted, and pathological alterations of this mechanism are implicated in auditory verbal hallucinations (Ford et al., 2001; Ozker et al., 2022; Khalilian-Gourtani et al., 2024). These principles mesh with "analysis-by-synthesis" accounts in which motor-invertible generative models propose candidate parses that are tested against incoming acoustics, enabling rapid recovery from noise and coarticulation (Bever & Poeppel, 2010; Hovsepyan et al., 2020).

Orthography piggybacks on ventral visual pathways via a reproducible "visual word form" zone in left ventral occipito-temporal cortex that becomes tuned through literacy, then couples to phonology and semantics along dorsal and ventral language tracts (Dehaene & Cohen, 2011; Price, 2012). This "neuronal recycling" view predicts modality-invariant higher language circuits with culture-specific front ends-the data broadly support that reading recruits the same inferior frontal and temporal-parietal combinatorial/lexical systems that support speech and sign.

Signed languages recruit left perisylvian cortex-including classical temporal and inferior frontal territories-despite visuomotor input/output, demonstrating that the combinatorial/semantic core is largely modality independent. Additional recruitment of dorsal parietofrontal visuomotor circuits reflects effector-specific demands (MacSweeney et al., 2008). This convergence constrains computational theories: linguistic composition and semantic mapping are properties of a fronto-temporal network that tolerates different sensorimotor interfaces.

Natural stories reveal a cortical gradient of temporal receptive windows: early auditory areas integrate over tens to hundreds of milliseconds, mid-level language areas over seconds, and default-mode subsystems (angular gyrus, posterior cingulate/precuneus, medial PFC, anterior temporal pole) integrate over tens of seconds to minutes, tracking paragraphs and situation models (Lerner et al., 2011). Information flow lags during narrative comprehension are consistent with feedforward accumulation of context followed by top-down constraint, elucidating how meaning is maintained and updated across long spans (Chang et al., 2022). Neural similarity across listeners in DMN predicts shared interpretations, quantifying when high-level priors converge. These findings situate language within the brain’s hierarchy of intrinsic timescales and explain why semantic hubs and DMN nodes are essential for inference beyond the sentence. Human single-neuron recordings provide a complementary view of semantic coding (Figure) 4. A human single-neuron study examines semantic responses to speech (Figure).

Language-selective fronto-temporal regions dissociate from the multiple-demand (MD) network: MD regions scale with task difficulty and executive demands but do not closely track linguistic content during passive comprehension; the adjacent language-selective territories in IFG and temporal cortex do (Fedorenko et al., 2012; Blank et al., 2014; Diachek et al., 2020). This dissociation clarifies how attention and control shape language without implementing core composition: MD and salience systems gate when/where resources are deployed, whereas the language network computes structure and meaning. For algorithmic models, this argues for a dual-route controller that modulates, but does not replace, specialized parsing/unification machinery.

Beyond cortex, cortico-basal ganglia-thalamic loops contribute to chunking and serial order selection-functions that map naturally onto morpho-phonological sequencing and prosodic timing-while cerebellar circuits provide forward-model predictions and event-based temporal calibration for speech perception and semantic expectations (Kotz & Schwartze, 2010/2016; Moberget & Ivry, 2016; Lesage et al., 2017; Jin & Costa, 2014). These loops are engaged even in the absence of overt movement, consistent with internal modeling roles; they intervene when language demands fast, precise temporal control (e.g., parsing time-compressed speech or maintaining meter), aligning with broad evidence that BG and cerebellum implement complementary timing/sequence control regimes.

A synthesis across EEG/MEG suggests a working division of labor: theta power tracks lexical/episodic retrieval; beta indexes maintenance of the current syntactic/semantic state and top-down predictions; gamma reflects local binding and mismatch repair, with task-/context-dependent variability (Bastiaansen & Hagoort, 2006; Lewis & Bastiaansen, 2015; Prystauka & Lewis, 2019). This is consistent with predictive-coding views in which beta carries top-down priors within the language network and gamma carries bottom-up error, coordinating dorsal buffers with ventral semantic composition in sentence/discourse processing.

For comprehension of a spoken sentence, bilateral auditory cortex entrains to prosodic and syllabic rhythms, chunking the stream; left posterior STG/STS and Spt transform acoustic features into phonological items while a dorsal phonological buffer maintains order; ventral temporal cortex maps items onto lexical-semantic candidates; IFG/ATL unify these into structured meaning; DMN nodes carry the situation model over long spans; and MD control engages when ambiguity, noise, or task rules require extra effort. Forward models from frontal-premotor speech systems send predictions to auditory cortex to cancel self-generated or expected input; deviations drive error signals that update lexical and structural hypotheses. During production, the same representational substrates are traversed in reverse: conceptual intent in DMN/temporal hubs selects lemmas; IFG unifies morpho-syntax; dorsal stream retrieves phonology and sequences syllables; motor cortex issues articulatory programs; auditory cortex compares expected and actual feedback and corrects online. This loop-level account explains rapid robustness in noise, human-like error patterns under dorsal lesions (phonological), and deep-semantics deficits under ATL damage, providing algorithmic constraints for AGI-scale language systems that must operate under uncertainty, across timescales, and with tight perception-action coupling (Hickok & Poeppel, 2007; Hagoort, 2013; Giraud & Poeppel, 2012; Ding et al., 2016; Kutas & Federmeier, 2011; Blank et al., 2014; Diachek et al., 2020).

The linguistic system achieves data efficiency and reliability by combining a specialized, composition-first representational substrate (fronto-temporal language network) with multi-timescale priors (temporal integration gradient reaching into DMN), error-driven prediction (auditory-motor loops with corollary discharge), and executive gating (MD/salience). For engineering, that suggests language modules that (i) implement explicit composition and long-context situation modeling, (ii) are embedded in active generative loops that predict and compare sensory consequences of candidate parses, (iii) maintain dorsal-style phonological buffers for serialization, and (iv) coordinate with domain-general controllers that regulate effort rather than perform parsing. These constraints are borne out by convergent anatomy, timing, and perturbation data and align with predictive-coding and analysis-by-synthesis frameworks that already scale in machine systems.
